newsitem.title: JAPAN: US, Jpn car makers mouth off on dlr, dealers ignore.
newsitem.headline: US, Jpn car makers mouth off on dlr, dealers ignore.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese automakers are having a war of words over the appropriate level for the dollar against the yen, but dealers here say Japan's burgeoning trade surplus, more than anything, will determine its fate.

Currency dealers shrugged off the rate predictions from top auto officials from both sides of the Pacific as Washington and Tokyo are unlikely to allow the companies to dictate policy and use foreign exchange rates as a tool of trade policy.
"Obviously, U.S. and Japanese makers have different opinions over the dollar, but their comments are not so important," said Yoh Nihei, a manager at Sakura Bank.

"More than that, the market reacted sensitively to the actual results of Japanese current account growth," Nihei said. "The market saw the facts (that the surplus was growing) and actively sold the dollar above 113 yen."

The dollar was put under downward pressure throughout the day in Tokyo on Wednesday, staying below 113 yen shortly after the release of the data showing Japan's current account surplus soared 155 percent in May, while the impact of comments by car makers was limited, Tokyo dealers said.

The Finance Ministry said on Wednesday that the current account surplus, often a source of bitter rows with the United States, jumped 154.9 percent in May to 906.8 billion yen ($8.02 billion at Wednesday's rate of around 113 yen to the dollar).
The surplus in merchandise trade alone surged 118.6 percent from a year earlier to 927.9 billion ($8.21 billion).

Ford Motor Co vice-chairman Wayne Booker, who was attending a meeting of the Japan-U.S. Business Council in San Francisco, said that a more appropriate dollar/yen exchange rate would be in the range of 100 to 110 yen.
An executive from General Motors Co was quoted as saying that the dollar should be around 105 yen.
Meanwhile, in Tokyo, Toyota Motor Corp president Hiroshi Okuda said an appropriate dollar/yen rate for the Japanese car industry was still 110-120 yen to the dollar.
Asked about Booker's range, Okuda said: "That level of the yen is too high."
Dealers said the market is not expected to react greatly unless top officials from Japan and the United States start expressing concern about the currency rates.

On Tuesday, Japan's most influential currency official acted to stave off speculation about the rising yen, saying Tokyo has not changed its foreign exchange policy despite its growing trade surplus with the United States.
"The MOF's (Ministry of Finance's) forex policy has not changed," said Eisuke Sakakibara, who has been dubbed "Mr Yen" because of his influence over currency markets.

"I understand that frustration is growing among U.S. car makers, but the market is not expecting the U.S. government to do anything for the industry right away," said Taisuke Tanaka, a strategist at Credit Suisse in Tokyo.
"The market will react if the U.S. government starts to express concern about the strong dollar against the yen," Tanaka said.
